chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Hasan al-Sayqal, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'A man prays the two rak'at of the Witr, then stands up and forgets the Tashahhud until he bows, and remembers while he is bowing.' He said, 'He should sit from his bowing, perform the Tashahhud, then stand up and complete (the prayer).'

I said, 'Did you not say regarding the obligatory prayer, that if he remembers it after having bowed, he should continue, then perform two prostrations of forgetfulness (Sajdatay al-Sahw) after he finishes, and perform the Tashahhud in them?' He said, 'The optional prayer is not like the obligatory prayer.'

key_terms.التَّشَهُّد: Tashahhud (the testimony of faith and blessings recited while sitting in prayer)
key_terms.الْوَتْر: Witr (the odd-numbered night prayer, typically three rak'at)
key_terms.سَجْدَتَيِ السَّهْو: Sajdatay al-Sahw (the two prostrations of forgetfulness)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if one forgets the Tashahhud during the Witr prayer and remembers while bowing?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies a key jurisprudential distinction between obligatory (Fard) and optional (Nafl) prayers, ruling that in the latter, forgetting the Tashahhud during Ruku' requires an immediate return to sitting to recite it, rather than continuing and performing prostrations of forgetfulness (Sujud al-Sahw) later. This highlights the Shia scholarly view that the procedural strictness of Nafl prayers often differs from Fard prayers, emphasizing precision in voluntary acts of worship. The ruling underscores the principle that while both require correctness, the mechanisms for correcting errors vary based on the prayer's nature.
